source.text: Εἴ τις οὖν παράκλησις ἐν Χριστῷ, εἴ τι παραμύθιον ἀγάπης, εἴ τις κοινωνία πνεύματος, εἴ τις σπλάγχνα καὶ οἰκτιρμοί, πληρώσατέ μου τὴν χαρὰν ἵνα τὸ αὐτὸ φρονῆτε, τὴν αὐτὴν ἀγάπην ἔχοντες, σύμψυχοι, τὸ ἓν φρονοῦντες, μηδὲν κατ’ ἐριθείαν μηδὲ κατὰ κενοδοξίαν, ἀλλὰ τῇ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ ἀλλήλους ἡγούμενοι ὑπερέχοντας ἑαυτῶν, μὴ τὰ ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστοι σκοποῦντες, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἑτέρων ἕκαστοι.

records.literal_gloss: If [there is] any therefore encouragement in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of [the] Spirit, if any affections and compassions, \v 2 fill of me the joy, so that the same you may think, the same love having, united in soul, the one thing thinking, \v 3 nothing according to selfish rivalry nor according to empty glory, but in the humility one another counting surpassing yourselves, \v 4 not the things of yourselves each looking to, but also the things of others each.

en.L: If then [there is] any encouragement in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of [the] Spirit, if any affection and compassion, \v 2 make my joy full, so that you think the same thing, having the same love, united in soul, thinking the one thing, \v 3 [doing] nothing out of selfish rivalry or out of empty glory, but in humility counting one another as surpassing yourselves, \v 4 each not looking to your own things, but each also to the things of others.
en.B: So if being in {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} gives you any encouragement, if love brings you any comfort, if you share at all in the Spirit, if you have any tender affection and compassion, \v 2 then fill my joy to the brim: be of one mind, hold on to the same love, be united in heart, and set your minds on one aim. \v 3 Do not act out of rivalry or out of a craving for empty glory. Instead, be humble, and regard each other as standing above yourselves. \v 4 Each of you should care not just about your own concerns but about the concerns of others as well.
en.R: You belong to {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, and that encourages you. Love comforts you. You share in the Spirit together. You have tender, caring hearts. \v 2 So make me completely full of joy by thinking in the same way. Love each other in the same way, and be united in heart and purpose. \v 3 Do not do anything just to beat others or to make yourselves look important. Be humble, and treat others as more important than yourselves. \v 4 Each of you should care about what matters to other people, not only about what matters to you.

decisions.choice: real conditions that Paul assumes are true: since there is
alternatives: open questions: if there is any, which may not be so
decisions.reason: The four clauses with Εἴ / εἴ use the form of condition that takes the "if" as fact. Paul is not doubting that the Philippians have these things; he is reminding them that they do, as the ground for his appeal in verse 2. The repeated "if" also gives the appeal its force, so the Literal and Balanced levels keep it.

decisions.choice: fellowship given by the Holy Spirit: a shared part in the Spirit
alternatives: a fellowship of spirit: human closeness, team spirit
the fellowship that the Spirit creates among believers (without the sense of sharing in the Spirit)
decisions.reason: πνεύματος has no article and could mean the human spirit. But the first clause names Christ, and Paul elsewhere speaks of "the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" (2 Corinthians 13:14). κοινωνία means having a share in something together: believers share in the one Spirit, and that sharing binds them to each other. The capital S marks this reading; a footnote gives the other.

decisions.choice: deep, warm affection and pity
decisions.reason: σπλάγχνα are literally the inner organs, which Greek speakers treated as the seat of the feelings, much as we speak of the heart. Paul used the word in 1:8 for his own longing for the Philippians. The second word is compassion for someone in need.

decisions.choice: "any" agrees with no noun: a fixed "if there is any"
decisions.reason: In this fourth clause the word for "any" is masculine singular, though the noun after it is neuter plural, so it does not match. The phrase works as a set formula repeated from the first three clauses. Some later manuscripts correct the form; the meaning is the same either way.

decisions.choice: a shared way of thinking and setting one's mind
decisions.reason: φρονέω, used twice here, is a key word in this letter: it means a whole outlook and attitude (compare 2:5 and 4:2). Paul asks for one mind about what matters, not agreement on every detail. σύμψυχοι, "one-souled", occurs only here in the New Testament.

decisions.choice: selfish rivalry; a hunger for empty honor
decisions.reason: The first word is the self-seeking party spirit Paul named in 1:17, when some preached Christ out of rivalry. The second is literally "empty glory": wanting praise that has nothing behind it.

decisions.choice: humbly giving others the higher place
alternatives: believing that everyone else is better than you in every way
decisions.reason: ταπεινοφροσύνῃ is a lowly view of oneself, a word Greek writers usually used as an insult; Paul makes it a virtue. ἡγούμενοι is a deliberate judgment: treat the other person as ranking above you. It is not a claim about who is more gifted, and verse 4 explains it as caring for others' interests. The same verb is used of Christ in verse 6 (ἡγήσατο), and verse 8 says he humbled himself: the hymn shows the attitude these verses ask for.

decisions.choice: not only one's own interests, but others' as well
alternatives: never one's own interests, only others'
decisions.reason: The "also" (καὶ) matters: Paul does not forbid caring for oneself, but he does not let it be the only concern. τὰ ἑαυτῶν, "their own things", returns in 2:21.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: four plain statements in place of four "if" clauses
decisions.reason: Readers of Readable may take "if" as doubt. Following meaning decision m1, Readable states the four things as facts, then gives the appeal with "So". It also says what "in Christ" means: belonging to him.

decisions.choice: empty glory
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the parts of the Greek compound, so the reader can see the contrast with the glory of God in verse 11. Readable says what it means: wanting to look important.

source.text: τοῦτο φρονεῖτε ἐν ὑμῖν ὃ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ὃς ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων οὐχ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ, ἀλλὰ ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν μορφὴν δούλου λαβών, ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος· καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου, θανάτου δὲ σταυροῦ·

records.literal_gloss: This think among you which also in Christ Jesus, \v 6 who in form of God existing not a thing seized considered the to be equal with God, \v 7 but himself emptied, form of a slave having taken, in likeness of human beings having come to be; and in appearance having been found as a human being \v 8 he humbled himself, having become obedient as far as death, of death but of a cross.

en.L: Think this among you, which [was] also in {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus, \v 6 who, existing in [the] form of God, did not consider being equal with God a thing to exploit, \v 7 but emptied {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, having taken [the] form of a slave, having come to be in [the] likeness of {{gender:human beings|men}}; and having been found in appearance as a human being, \v 8 {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} humbled {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, having become obedient as far as death, even death of a cross.
en.B: Among yourselves, think in the way that {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus also thought, \v 6 who, being in the form of God, did not treat being equal with God as something to exploit for {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}. \v 7 Rather, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} emptied {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, taking on the form of a servant and coming to share the likeness of {{gender:human beings|men}}. And when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was found in outward form as a human being, \v 8 {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} humbled {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, becoming obedient all the way to death, death on a cross.
en.R: Think in the same way that {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus thought. \v 6 {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} was in the form of God, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not use being equal with God for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own benefit. \v 7 Instead, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} emptied {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} took the form of a servant and was born as a human being. In every way people could see, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was a human being. \v 8 And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} humbled {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} by obeying God all the way to death, even death on a cross.

decisions.choice: the way of thinking that was also in Christ Jesus: his own example
alternatives: the way of thinking you have (or: that is fitting) in Christ Jesus: the outlook that belongs to those who are united with him
decisions.reason: The Greek has no verb in this clause, so one must be supplied. Read with "was", Paul points to Christ's own attitude, which the next verses describe step by step: he did not look to his own interests (compare 2:4) and he humbled himself (compare 2:3). The other reading supplies "you think" or "is fitting": think among yourselves the way you think as people who are in Christ Jesus. That fits the way Paul usually uses "in Christ" (as in 4:7) for being united with him. Both readings make good sense, and both lead to the hymn; a footnote gives the other.

decisions.choice: among you: in your life together
decisions.reason: The "you" is plural, and the whole appeal (2:1-4) is about how the church treats one another. The phrase can also mean in each person's own mind; the two go together.

decisions.choice: verses 6-11 read as a poem or hymn
decisions.reason: These verses fall into short, balanced lines, unlike the prose around them. Whether Paul wrote them himself or quoted words the churches already knew cannot be known. Either way he uses them as the example for verses 3-4: the one who was highest made himself lowest.

decisions.choice: in the form of God: having God's own way of being, seen in his status and glory
alternatives: the image of God, as in Adam (Genesis 1:27)
decisions.reason: μορφῇ is the form in which something truly appears, not a disguise. It is paired with "the form of a slave" in verse 7: Christ was as truly in God's form as he was truly a slave. ὑπάρχων ("existing") describes what he already was before he emptied himself. The phrase does not by itself define how Christ relates to the Father; the next clause calls it being equal with God.

decisions.choice: though he was in the form of God
alternatives: because he was in the form of God, he did not ...
decisions.reason: The participle gives the setting for what follows, and the "but" in verse 7 sets what he had against what he did, so "though" is the natural reading. It can also be read "because": being in God's form is the reason he gave himself, which says something about what God is like. Balanced keeps "being", which allows both.

decisions.choice: something to exploit: he did not use his equality with God for his own advantage
alternatives: something to seize: he did not try to grab equality with God, which he did not yet have
something to cling to: he did not hold on to equality with God, but let it go
decisions.reason: ἁρπαγμὸν comes from the verb "to seize" and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, so its sense must come from context. The verse has just said he already existed in God's form, and the article before "to be equal" points back to that, so the question is not whether he would grab equality but what he would do with it. Verses 3-4 (not looking to one's own interests) and verse 7 (he emptied himself) point to the answer: he did not treat it as something to use for himself. The reading "seize" contrasts Christ with Adam, who reached to be like God (Genesis 3:5); the reading "cling to" also fits verse 7. The words leave room for each, so a footnote gives them.

decisions.choice: emptied himself: made himself nothing, by taking a slave's form and becoming human
alternatives: emptied himself of his divine nature
emptied himself of some divine powers or privileges
decisions.reason: ἐκένωσεν means to make empty or of no account. Paul does not say what Christ emptied himself of; he says how: the two phrases that follow, taking a slave's form and coming to be in human likeness. The emptying is giving, not losing: the one in the form of God took on the form of a slave. Theories about which divine powers Christ set aside go beyond what the verse says, so the translation keeps the bare words "emptied himself".

decisions.choice: slave
decisions.reason: δούλου is the ordinary word for a slave, someone owned by another and without rights. It stands opposite "form of God" here and opposite "Lord" in verse 11. Paul and Timothy call themselves slaves of Christ Jesus in 1:1.

decisions.choice: truly human, as others saw him
alternatives: a male, as opposed to a woman
decisions.reason: ὁμοιώματι (likeness) does not mean a mere appearance: Paul uses it in Romans 8:3, where God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. σχήματι is the outward bearing others could see: in everything visible he was a human being. The word for human being here is the general one; the point is that he shared our humanity, not his maleness.

decisions.choice: he humbled himself by obeying God, as far as death
alternatives: obedient to death, as if death were his master
decisions.reason: ἐταπείνωσεν is the verb of the noun "humility" in verse 3. The obedience is to God; the text does not say so in words, but there is no one else he could be obeying. "As far as death" measures how far his obedience went. The same phrase is used of Epaphroditus in 2:30.

decisions.choice: crucifixion: the most shameful death
decisions.reason: Rome used crucifixion for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals; Roman citizens, as many in Philippi were, were normally exempt from it. The Law also said that one hanged on a tree is under God's curse (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). The slave's form of verse 7 ends in a slave's death.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting. The sentence is arranged so that no such pronoun starts an English sentence, where the two options would look the same.

decisions.choice: {{gender:human beings|men}}
decisions.reason: The plural is the general word for people, so the gender setting applies: the inclusive default, with the traditional "men" one tap away.

decisions.choice: a human being, no setting
decisions.reason: The singular here refers to Christ, a specific man, and the guide never puts a gender setting on Christ. The word's sense in this verse is a human being (meaning decision m9), so every reader sees that.

decisions.choice: was born as a human being; obeying God
alternatives: came to be in human likeness; becoming obedient
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "coming to be in human likeness" means (compare Galatians 4:4) and names God as the one Christ obeyed, which the Greek leaves implied (meaning decision m10).

decisions.choice: exploit (L, B); use for his own benefit (R)
decisions.reason: These follow meaning decision m6. "Grasp" is often used here, but it can mean either seize or cling to, and does not say what the context points to.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it and as is traditional here; the meaning decision (m8) keeps that this is the lowest status, one owned and without rights, set against the form of God, and Literal keeps "slave".

source.text: διὸ καὶ ὁ θεὸς αὐτὸν ὑπερύψωσεν, καὶ ἐχαρίσατο αὐτῷ τὸ ὄνομα τὸ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα, ἵνα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ πᾶν γόνυ κάμψῃ ἐπουρανίων καὶ ἐπιγείων καὶ καταχθονίων, καὶ πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολογήσηται ὅτι κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ πατρός.

records.literal_gloss: Therefore also the God him highly exalted and graciously gave to him the name the above every name, \v 10 so that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of heavenly [ones] and earthly [ones] and under-the-earth [ones], \v 11 and every tongue should confess that Lord [is] Jesus Christ, to glory of God Father.

en.L: Therefore God also highly exalted {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and graciously gave {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} the name that [is] above every name, \v 10 so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of [those] in heaven and on earth and under the earth, \v 11 and every tongue should confess that Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} [is] Lord, to [the] glory of God [the] Father.
en.B: That is why God has exalted {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} far above all and freely given {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} the name that is above every name, \v 10 so that every knee will bend before the name of Jesus, in heaven, on earth and below the earth, \v 11 and every tongue will openly declare that Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is Lord, bringing glory to God the Father.
en.R: So God lifted {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} up to the highest honor and gave {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} the name that is greater than every other name. \v 10 God did this so that everyone in heaven, on earth, and under the earth will kneel down to honor the name of Jesus, \v 11 and everyone will say out loud that Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is Lord. This will bring glory to God the Father.

decisions.choice: for this reason: God's answer to Christ's self-humbling
decisions.reason: The turn comes at διὸ: until now Christ has been the one acting; from here God acts. The one who lowered himself is lifted up, as Jesus taught (Matthew 23:12).

decisions.choice: exalted above all; an echo of the Servant in Isaiah 52:13
decisions.reason: The verb is a strengthened form of "lift up, exalt", meaning raised beyond all others. The Greek of Isaiah 52:13 uses the simple form of the same verb of the Lord's Servant, the one who is then humbled to death (Isaiah 53), as Christ is in verses 7-8.

decisions.choice: the name above every name is "Lord"
alternatives: the name "Jesus", now honored above every other name
decisions.reason: In the Bible a name stands for a person's rank and character. Verse 11 says what every tongue will confess: that Jesus Christ is Lord. That is the title God gives him, the one that ranks above every other. "Jesus" in verse 10 is the person who bears it. The verb for giving is the one used for a free gift, from the same root as grace.

decisions.choice: every knee will bow, every tongue confess: Isaiah 45:23
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 45:22-23 the LORD says that he alone is God, and that to him every knee will bow and every tongue will swear. Paul echoes the wording of the Greek translation of that verse, and applies to Jesus the honor that Isaiah says belongs to God alone. Paul quotes the same verse of God in Romans 14:11.

decisions.choice: Lord: the title that the Greek Old Testament gives to God
alternatives: lord: a master or ruler, a title of respect
decisions.reason: κύριος can be a polite "sir" or a slave's master, which would contrast with the slave of verse 7. But in the Greek translation of the Old Testament that Paul quotes, it stands in place of God's own name, the LORD, and the echo of Isaiah 45 here makes that sense clear. Yet the confession is "to the glory of God the Father": giving Jesus this name does not take glory from the Father. "Jesus Christ is Lord" was the earliest Christian confession of faith (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3).

decisions.choice: in honor of the name of Jesus
alternatives: whenever the name of Jesus is spoken
praying in the name of Jesus
decisions.reason: ἐν here gives the one the knees bow to. It is about honoring the person whose name it is, not a gesture at the sound of a word.

decisions.choice: all beings in heaven, on earth and in the realm of the dead
decisions.reason: The three words name every part of creation as the ancient world pictured it: heaven, earth, and the world of the dead below it. No one is left out.

decisions.choice: God's purpose, which will surely be done
alternatives: a promise that every being will be saved
decisions.reason: ἵνα states the goal of God's exaltation of Jesus: in the end every creature will acknowledge him. The verse states that this will happen; it does not say whether all will do so willingly. Isaiah 45:24 goes on to speak of those who were angry with God being put to shame.

decisions.choice: Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: exalted far above all (B); lifted up to the highest honor (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means raised beyond everyone else; Balanced and Readable say that in ordinary words.

decisions.choice: everyone will kneel down; everyone will say out loud
alternatives: every knee will bow; every tongue will confess
decisions.reason: Readable turns the picture of knees and tongues into the people who kneel and speak. Literal and Balanced keep the wording that echoes Isaiah 45:23.

source.text: Ὥστε, ἀγαπητοί μου, καθὼς πάντοτε ὑπηκούσατε, μὴ ὡς ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ μου μόνον ἀλλὰ νῦν πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἐν τῇ ἀπουσίᾳ μου, μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου τὴν ἑαυτῶν σωτηρίαν κατεργάζεσθε, θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἐν ὑμῖν καὶ τὸ θέλειν καὶ τὸ ἐνεργεῖν ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας.

records.literal_gloss: So then, beloved of me, just as always you obeyed, not as in the presence of me only but now much more in the absence of me, with fear and trembling the of yourselves salvation work out; \v 13 God for is the [one] working in you both the to will and the to work for the good pleasure.

en.L: So then, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, with fear and trembling work out your own salvation; \v 13 for God is the one working in you both to will and to work, for [{{deity_pronoun:his|His}}] good pleasure.
en.B: So then, my beloved, you have always obeyed. Keep at it now, not only as if I were there with you, but much more because I am away: with fear and trembling, keep working out your own salvation. \v 13 For it is God who is at work in you, producing both the wanting and the doing, for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own good pleasure.
en.R: So, my dear friends, you have always obeyed. Keep on obeying, not only as you did when I was with you, but even more now that I am away. Keep working out your own salvation, with deep awe and respect for God. \v 13 God is the one who is at work in you. God gives you the desire to do what pleases {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and the power to do it.

decisions.choice: "not only in my presence" goes with the command to work out salvation
decisions.reason: μὴ is the "not" used with commands, so the phrase belongs to the command at the end of the verse: whether Paul is there or not, keep on. "You have always obeyed" is the example they are to keep following. Their obedience echoes Christ's in verse 8, where the related word "obedient" is used.

decisions.choice: work out: carry through to its goal the salvation God has given
alternatives: work out the well-being of your church
decisions.reason: κατεργάζεσθε means to carry something through to completion. It cannot mean earning salvation: the next verse says God is the one at work in them, and 1:6 says God will finish the good work he began. Salvation here is God's whole saving work, which they live out in their conduct until the day of Christ (1:28, 3:20-21). The "you" is plural, so they do this together, which ties the verse to the appeal for unity in verses 1-4.

decisions.choice: with deep reverence and humility before God
decisions.reason: "Fear and trembling" is a stock phrase for serious, humble reverence: Paul uses it of his own coming to Corinth (1 Corinthians 2:3) and of how slaves should serve (Ephesians 6:5). Psalm 2:11 calls for serving the LORD with fear and rejoicing with trembling. It is not dread of being rejected; verse 13 gives the reason for it.

decisions.choice: they work because God works in them
decisions.reason: γάρ gives the ground of the command. ἐνεργῶν and ἐνεργεῖν are the same verb: God is the one at work, and he works in them both the wish and the action. Their working out does not compete with his working in.

decisions.choice: for God's good pleasure: to do what pleases him
alternatives: for the sake of goodwill among you
decisions.reason: εὐδοκίας is pleasure or good will. The article points to the one just named, God, as in Luke 2:14 and Ephesians 1:5. The word can also mean human goodwill (as in 1:15), but here God is the subject of the sentence.

decisions.choice: with deep awe and respect for God
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom (meaning decision m3), and names God, whom the reverence is for; Literal and Balanced keep the phrase.

decisions.choice: keep working out
decisions.reason: The present command means a continuing task; "keep" says so.

source.text: Πάντα ποιεῖτε χωρὶς γογγυσμῶν καὶ διαλογισμῶν, ἵνα γένησθε ἄμεμπτοι καὶ ἀκέραιοι, τέκνα θεοῦ ἄμωμα μέσον γενεᾶς σκολιᾶς καὶ διεστραμμένης, ἐν οἷς φαίνεσθε ὡς φωστῆρες ἐν κόσμῳ λόγον ζωῆς ἐπέχοντες, εἰς καύχημα ἐμοὶ εἰς ἡμέραν Χριστοῦ, ὅτι οὐκ εἰς κενὸν ἔδραμον οὐδὲ εἰς κενὸν ἐκοπίασα.

records.literal_gloss: All things do without grumblings and disputes, \v 15 so that you may become blameless and pure, children of God without blemish in midst of a generation crooked and distorted, among whom you shine as lights in [the] world, \v 16 [the] word of life holding fast, for a boast to me in [the] day of Christ, that not in vain I ran nor in vain I labored.

en.L: Do all things without grumblings and disputes, \v 15 so that you may become blameless and pure, children of God without blemish in [the] midst of a crooked and distorted generation, among whom you shine as lights in [the] world, \v 16 holding fast [the] word of life, for a boast to me in [the] day of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, that I did not run in vain nor labor in vain.
en.B: In all you do, avoid complaining and quarreling, \v 15 so that no one can fault you and you stay pure, God's children without blemish in the midst of a crooked and distorted generation. Among these people you shine like stars in the world \v 16 as you keep a firm grip on the word of life. That way, when the day of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} comes, I can be proud that my running was not wasted and my hard work was not wasted.
en.R: Do everything without complaining or quarreling. \v 15 Then no one will be able to blame you, and you will be pure. You will be God's children with nothing wrong in you, living among the crooked and dishonest people of your time. Among them you shine like stars in the world, \v 16 as you hold on tightly to the message that gives life. Then on the day {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} returns, I will be proud of you. I will know that all my running and hard work were not wasted.

decisions.choice: grumbling, like Israel in the wilderness
decisions.reason: γογγυσμῶν is the word family the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel's complaining against God and Moses in the desert (Exodus 16:7-12; Numbers 14:27). Paul has just spoken of obedience (verse 12), and the next verse quotes Moses' song: the Philippians are not to repeat Israel's story.

decisions.choice: disputes, quarrels
decisions.reason: The word can mean arguments or private doubts. After 2:1-4, and with Euodia and Syntyche in mind (4:2), disputes with one another are meant.

decisions.choice: Deuteronomy 32:5, reversed
decisions.reason: In the song of Moses the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:5 says Israel sinned, children who were not his, blemished, "a crooked and distorted generation". Paul uses those words but reverses them: the Philippians are to be God's children without blemish in the middle of such a generation. "Without blemish" is also the word for a sacrifice with no defect.

decisions.choice: you shine like the lights of the sky
decisions.reason: φωστῆρες are the sun, moon and stars: the same word names the lights God set in the sky in the Greek of Genesis 1:14-16. Daniel 12:3 says the wise will shine like the brightness of the sky. The verb states a fact ("you shine"), not a command; it describes what they are among that generation.

decisions.choice: holding fast the word of life
alternatives: holding out the word of life: offering it to the world
decisions.reason: ἐπέχοντες can mean holding firmly to something or holding it out to others. "Holding out" fits the picture of lights shining in the world. "Holding fast" fits what follows: Paul will be proud on the day of Christ because they stood firm, proving his work was not wasted, and he urged them in 1:27 to stand firm. Both senses are possible and the evidence is close; a footnote gives the other.

decisions.choice: the message that brings life: the gospel
alternatives: Christ, the Word who is life
decisions.reason: Paul uses "the word" for the gospel message (1:14). ζωῆς is the life that the message gives.

decisions.choice: running and labor for nothing: wasted effort
decisions.reason: Running is the athlete's image Paul uses for his work (Galatians 2:2; 1 Corinthians 9:24-27; Philippians 3:14). "To labor in vain" is also the Servant's complaint in Isaiah 49:4. Paul's boast on the day of Christ will be the Philippians themselves (compare 4:1).

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: distorted (L, B); dishonest (R)
decisions.reason: The word means turned aside or bent out of shape. "Distorted" keeps that picture without the narrower modern sense of "perverse".

decisions.choice: stars
decisions.reason: Following meaning decision m4, the lights are the lights of the sky; "stars" makes that picture clear at night, when stars are what one sees shining.

decisions.choice: the day the Messiah returns
decisions.reason: Readable explains "the day of Christ": the day he comes again (1:6, 1:10; 3:20).

source.text: ἀλλὰ εἰ καὶ σπένδομαι ἐπὶ τῇ θυσίᾳ καὶ λειτουργίᾳ τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν, χαίρω καὶ συγχαίρω πᾶσιν ὑμῖν·

records.literal_gloss: But if even I am poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice and service of the faith of you, I rejoice and I rejoice with all you;

en.L: But even if I am being poured out as a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and rejoice together with you all;
en.B: And even if my life is being poured out like a drink offering over the sacrifice and priestly service that your faith offers, I am glad, and I share my joy with all of you.
en.R: Your faith and your service to God are like a sacrifice offered to God. My life may be poured out on it, like the wine that was poured out with a sacrifice. Even so, I am glad, and I am glad together with all of you.

decisions.choice: a drink offering: wine poured out with a sacrifice
decisions.reason: σπένδομαι is the verb for pouring out a drink offering. In Israel's worship wine was poured out with the burnt offerings (Numbers 15:1-10; 28:7), and Greeks and Romans also poured wine for their gods. Paul pictures his own life being poured out; he uses the same image near his death in 2 Timothy 4:6.

decisions.choice: even if my death comes, as it may
alternatives: even though I am already being poured out in my sufferings now
decisions.reason: "Even if" admits a real possibility. Paul is in prison awaiting a verdict that could mean his death (1:20-23), though he hopes to be freed (1:25, 2:24). The present tense may also include what he is suffering now.

decisions.choice: their faith, shown in service, is the sacrifice
alternatives: the sacrifice Paul offers is their faith
decisions.reason: The Philippians' faith, and their service that comes from it, are the sacrifice offered to God; Paul's life is the drink offering added to it. λειτουργίᾳ is a word for service done for the public or for God, used of priests; it returns in 2:25 and 2:30 for Epaphroditus' service to Paul on their behalf.

decisions.choice: share my joy with you
decisions.reason: συγχαίρω is to rejoice together with someone. Paul shares his gladness with them, and in the next verse asks them to share theirs with him.

decisions.choice: my life
decisions.reason: Greek says "I am poured out"; Balanced and Readable say "my life", because the image is of Paul giving his life.

decisions.choice: the sacrifice first, then Paul's offering
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture in two steps: first what the sacrifice is, then how Paul's life is poured out with it.

source.text: τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ καὶ ὑμεῖς χαίρετε καὶ συγχαίρετέ μοι.

records.literal_gloss: The and same also you rejoice and rejoice with me.

en.L: And in the same way you also, rejoice and rejoice together with me.
en.B: In the same way, you too should be glad and share your joy with me.
en.R: In the same way, you should be glad too, and share your gladness with me.

decisions.choice: a call: be glad and share it with me
alternatives: a statement: you also are glad
decisions.reason: χαίρετε and συγχαίρετέ can be read as statements or commands; the setting, after "I rejoice with you all", makes them a call to return Paul's joy. "The same" means in the same way.

decisions.choice: joy even in the face of Paul's possible death
decisions.reason: Paul asks them to be glad not in spite of his sacrifice but along with it, because his life is given for their faith. Joy runs through the whole letter (1:18; 3:1; 4:4).

source.text: Ἐλπίζω δὲ ἐν κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ Τιμόθεον ταχέως πέμψαι ὑμῖν, ἵνα κἀγὼ εὐψυχῶ γνοὺς τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν.

records.literal_gloss: I hope but in [the] Lord Jesus Timothy soon to send to you, so that I also may be cheered, having known the things about you.

en.L: Now I hope in [the] Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I also may be cheered, having learned the things about you.
en.B: I hope, in the Lord Jesus, to send Timothy to you before long, so that I too may be heartened when I hear news of you.
en.R: I hope, if the Lord Jesus allows, to send Timothy to you soon. Then I will be cheered up too, when I hear how you are doing.

decisions.choice: a hope that depends on the Lord Jesus
decisions.reason: Paul makes his plans as one who belongs to the Lord and depends on him; whether they happen is in the Lord's hands (compare 2:24 and James 4:15).

decisions.choice: Timothy, who helped found the church at Philippi
decisions.reason: Timothy joins Paul in sending this letter (1:1) and was with him when the church at Philippi began (Acts 16:1-12). The Philippians knew him well (verse 22).

decisions.choice: I too: as you will be by news of me
decisions.reason: κἀγὼ, "I also", assumes the Philippians will be encouraged by the news Timothy brings of Paul (verse 23); Paul hopes to be encouraged in return. The verb, to be in good spirits, occurs only here in the New Testament.

decisions.choice: if the Lord Jesus allows
decisions.reason: Readable explains what hoping "in the Lord Jesus" means here (meaning decision m1).

source.text: οὐδένα γὰρ ἔχω ἰσόψυχον ὅστις γνησίως τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν μεριμνήσει, οἱ πάντες γὰρ τὰ ἑαυτῶν ζητοῦσιν, οὐ τὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: No one for I have of equal soul who genuinely the things about you will care for; \v 21 the all for the things of themselves seek, not the things of Jesus Christ.

en.L: For I have no one of equal soul, who will genuinely care about the things concerning you; \v 21 for they all seek their own things, not the things of Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.
en.B: I have no one else of the same heart, no one who will truly care about your welfare. \v 21 The others are all pursuing their own concerns, not those of Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
en.R: There is no one else like Timothy. He truly cares about how you are doing. \v 21 Everyone else is looking out for themselves, not for what matters to Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: no one else like Timothy
alternatives: no one who shares my own heart as Timothy does
decisions.reason: ἰσόψυχον, "of equal soul", occurs only here in the New Testament, and Paul does not say equal to whom. The sentence is about why Timothy is the one to send, which suggests: no one else is like him. But it can mean no one else shares Paul's own heart for the Philippians, as Timothy does; verse 22 describes them as father and son. Either way, Timothy is the only one who cares as Paul does.

decisions.choice: genuine concern for others
decisions.reason: μεριμνήσει is the verb Paul uses in 4:6 for the anxiety he forbids. Here it is the good kind of care: Timothy's concern for the church.

decisions.choice: the others around Paul, not every Christian
decisions.reason: "They all" are those Paul could otherwise send. His sharp words echo 2:4: they look to their own things, the very phrase of that verse, while Timothy looks to the things of others.

decisions.choice: Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: no one else like Timothy
decisions.reason: Readable names Timothy so the reader knows who is being compared, following meaning decision m1.

source.text: τὴν δὲ δοκιμὴν αὐτοῦ γινώσκετε, ὅτι ὡς πατρὶ τέκνον σὺν ἐμοὶ ἐδούλευσεν εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον.

records.literal_gloss: The but proven worth of him you know, that as a father a child with me he served for the gospel.

en.L: But you know his proven worth, that as a child [serves] a father he served with me for the gospel.
en.B: But you know how he has proved himself: like a son working alongside his father, he has served with me in spreading the gospel.
en.R: And you know that Timothy has proven himself. He has worked with me to spread the good news, like a son working with his father.

decisions.choice: character proved by testing
decisions.reason: δοκιμὴν is worth that has been tested and shown to be genuine, like metal that passes the test. The Philippians had seen Timothy at work among them.

decisions.choice: he served with me, as a son works with his father
alternatives: he served me, as a son serves his father
decisions.reason: Paul begins a picture of a son serving his father, then changes it: Timothy served "with me". He is Paul's partner in the work, not his servant. ἐδούλευσεν is the verb of the word "slave", as in 1:1, and echoes Christ taking the form of a slave (2:7).

decisions.choice: for the gospel: to advance it
decisions.reason: εἰς gives the goal of their service: spreading the gospel, as in 1:5 and 1:12.

decisions.choice: son
decisions.reason: Timothy is a man, and the picture is of a son learning his father's trade; Literal keeps "child".

source.text: τοῦτον μὲν οὖν ἐλπίζω πέμψαι ὡς ἂν ἀφίδω τὰ περὶ ἐμὲ ἐξαυτῆς·

records.literal_gloss: This one indeed therefore I hope to send, whenever I see the things concerning me, at once;

en.L: Him, then, I hope to send at once, as soon as I see the things concerning me;
en.B: So he is the one I hope to send, right away, as soon as I see how things will turn out for me.
en.R: So I hope to send him to you as soon as I know what is going to happen to me.

decisions.choice: how my case turns out
decisions.reason: Paul is a prisoner awaiting a decision that could free him or put him to death (1:19-26). He wants to send Timothy with that news.

decisions.choice: at once: goes with sending
decisions.reason: The word comes last in the Greek sentence; it most naturally says Timothy will be sent without delay once the outcome is known.

source.text: πέποιθα δὲ ἐν κυρίῳ ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸς ταχέως ἐλεύσομαι.

records.literal_gloss: I am persuaded and in [the] Lord that also myself soon I will come.

en.L: And I am persuaded in [the] Lord that I myself also will come soon.
en.B: And I am convinced, trusting in the Lord, that I myself will also come before long.
en.R: And I trust the Lord that I will come to see you soon too.

decisions.choice: a confidence that rests on the Lord
decisions.reason: Paul's confidence is not a prediction from the facts of his case but trust in the Lord, as in 1:25. Whether he was released and came cannot be known from this letter.

decisions.choice: come to see you
decisions.reason: Readable says where Paul hopes to come.

source.text: Ἀναγκαῖον δὲ ἡγησάμην Ἐπαφρόδιτον τὸν ἀδελφὸν καὶ συνεργὸν καὶ συστρατιώτην μου, ὑμῶν δὲ ἀπόστολον καὶ λειτουργὸν τῆς χρείας μου, πέμψαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ἐπειδὴ ἐπιποθῶν ἦν πάντας ὑμᾶς, καὶ ἀδημονῶν διότι ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἠσθένησεν.

records.literal_gloss: Necessary but I considered Epaphroditus the brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier of me, of you and messenger and minister of the need of me, to send to you, \v 26 since longing he was for all you, and being deeply distressed because you heard that he was ill.

en.L: But I considered [it] necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need, \v 26 since he was longing for you all, and was deeply distressed because you heard that he was ill.
en.B: Even so, I have decided I must send Epaphroditus back to you. He is my brother, who has worked beside me and fought beside me, and he is your envoy, whom you sent to serve me in my need. \v 26 For he has been longing for all of you, and has been deeply upset that you heard he was ill.
en.R: But I think I should send Epaphroditus back to you now. He is my brother in the Lord. He has worked with me and fought at my side. You sent him to bring me what I needed and to take care of me. \v 26 He has been missing all of you very much. And he has been very upset because you heard that he was sick.

decisions.choice: I have decided to send him: he is carrying this letter
decisions.reason: The past tense is the one letter writers used for what would be past when the letter was read. Epaphroditus is going back to Philippi, most likely carrying this letter (compare 2:28).

decisions.choice: Epaphroditus, sent by the church at Philippi
decisions.reason: He brought the Philippians' gift to Paul in prison (4:18) and stayed to help him. He is named only in this letter.

decisions.choice: messenger, envoy: one sent by the church
alternatives: apostle, like the Twelve or Paul
decisions.reason: ἀπόστολον means someone sent with a mission. Here Epaphroditus is "your" envoy: sent by the Philippians, not appointed by Christ like the Twelve. Paul uses the word the same way in 2 Corinthians 8:23 for the envoys of the churches.

decisions.choice: one who serves on behalf of others, a sacred service
decisions.reason: λειτουργὸν was used of public servants and of priests. It links to the "service" of the Philippians' faith in 2:17 and to 2:30: Epaphroditus' care for Paul was an offering made on behalf of the whole church.

decisions.choice: fellow soldier: comrade in the struggle for the gospel
decisions.reason: Paul uses military images for the work of the gospel (1:27-30; Philemon 2). In Philippi, a Roman colony settled by veterans, the picture would be familiar.

decisions.choice: deeply distressed
decisions.reason: ἀδημονῶν is strong: it is the word used of Jesus' anguish in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:37; Mark 14:33). Epaphroditus was distressed not for himself but because his church was worried about him.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: longing for you all
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts add "to see". The meaning hardly changes, so there is no footnote.

decisions.choice: send back
decisions.reason: Epaphroditus came from Philippi, so sending him to them is sending him back.

decisions.choice: my brother in the Lord
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that "brother" means fellow believer, not a family member. No gender setting applies: the brother is one named man.

decisions.choice: envoy (B); you sent him (R)
decisions.reason: "Apostle" would suggest the office of the Twelve (meaning decision m3).

source.text: καὶ γὰρ ἠσθένησεν παραπλήσιον θανάτῳ· ἀλλὰ ὁ θεὸς ἠλέησεν αὐτόν, οὐκ αὐτὸν δὲ μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐμέ, ἵνα μὴ λύπην ἐπὶ λύπην σχῶ.

records.literal_gloss: And indeed he was ill near to death; but the God had mercy on him, not him and only but also me, so that not sorrow upon sorrow I might have.

en.L: For indeed he was ill, close to death; but God had mercy on him, and not on him only but also on me, so that I might not have sorrow upon sorrow.
en.B: He really was sick, so sick he almost died. But God showed him mercy, and not only him but me as well, so that I would not have grief on top of grief.
en.R: He was so sick that he nearly died. But God was kind to him and made him well. And God was kind to me too, so that I would not have one sorrow piled on top of another.

decisions.choice: God's mercy shown in his recovery
decisions.reason: ἠλέησεν is to have mercy or pity. The mercy was that Epaphroditus recovered; Paul does not say how, and does not treat the recovery as owed. He also counts his own relief as God's mercy to him.

decisions.choice: sorrow added to sorrow
decisions.reason: Paul already had sorrow (his imprisonment and the troubles of 1:15-17); the death of Epaphroditus would have added another. Grief at a believer's death is not wrong in Paul's eyes (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:13, where grief is to be with hope).

decisions.choice: made him well
decisions.reason: Readable says what the mercy was, which the context makes clear (meaning decision m1).

source.text: σπουδαιοτέρως οὖν ἔπεμψα αὐτὸν ἵνα ἰδόντες αὐτὸν πάλιν χαρῆτε κἀγὼ ἀλυπότερος ὦ.

records.literal_gloss: More eagerly therefore I sent him so that having seen him again you may rejoice and I less sorrowful may be.

en.L: I sent him therefore all the more eagerly, so that, having seen him again, you may rejoice, and I may be less sorrowful.
en.B: That is why I am sending him the more urgently, so that you can see him again and be glad, and I can have less sorrow.
en.R: So I am very eager to send him back to you. When you see him again, you will be happy, and I will not be so sad.

decisions.choice: I am sending him: he carries the letter
decisions.reason: As in verse 25, the past tense is written from the time the letter would be read.

decisions.choice: see him again
decisions.reason: πάλιν stands between "seeing him" and "rejoice" and could go with either. Since they had sent him away and he is coming back, "seeing him again" is the more natural reading; the sense is hardly affected.

decisions.choice: more eagerly, with greater urgency
decisions.reason: The word combines eagerness and haste. Paul sends him sooner than he might have, for the Philippians' sake.

decisions.choice: less sorrow for me
decisions.reason: Paul's sorrow will lessen because their worry is over, and perhaps because he will no longer be the cause of Epaphroditus' absence from home.

decisions.choice: I am sending
decisions.reason: Following meaning decision m1.

source.text: προσδέχεσθε οὖν αὐτὸν ἐν κυρίῳ μετὰ πάσης χαρᾶς, καὶ τοὺς τοιούτους ἐντίμους ἔχετε, ὅτι διὰ τὸ ἔργον Χριστοῦ μέχρι θανάτου ἤγγισεν, παραβολευσάμενος τῇ ψυχῇ ἵνα ἀναπληρώσῃ τὸ ὑμῶν ὑστέρημα τῆς πρός με λειτουργίας.

records.literal_gloss: Receive therefore him in [the] Lord with all joy, and the such ones in honor hold, \v 30 because for the sake of the work of Christ as far as death he came near, having gambled with the life so that he might fill up the of you lack of the toward me service.

en.L: Receive him therefore in [the] Lord with all joy, and hold such [people] in honor, \v 30 because for the sake of the work of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} he came near as far as death, having gambled with [his] life, so that he might fill up your lack of service toward me.
en.B: So receive him in the Lord with complete joy, and hold people like him in high regard. \v 30 He came to the edge of death for the work of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, staking his life so that he could supply what was missing in your service to me.
en.R: So welcome him with great joy, as people who belong to the Lord. Show honor to people like him. \v 30 He nearly died while doing the work of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. He put his life in danger to give me the help that you could not give me yourselves, because you were far away.

decisions.choice: welcome him as fellow believers welcome one of their own
decisions.reason: "In the Lord" means as people who belong to the Lord. Paul may be heading off any thought that Epaphroditus came home early or failed in his task.

decisions.choice: as far as death: the same words used of Christ
decisions.reason: μέχρι θανάτου is the phrase of 2:8, where Christ was obedient as far as death. Epaphroditus, like Timothy before him, follows the pattern of the hymn: he risked everything for others' sake.

decisions.choice: risking his life: staking it like a gambler
decisions.reason: παραβολευσάμενος comes from the language of betting: to stake something, to expose it to risk. It occurs only here in the New Testament. Epaphroditus put his life on the line.

decisions.choice: he did in person what the church could not do from far away
alternatives: a rebuke: the Philippians had failed to help Paul
decisions.reason: The "lack" is not a fault in their giving, which Paul praises (4:10-18). The only thing missing was their being there; Epaphroditus served Paul on the whole church's behalf. λειτουργίας again uses the word for sacred service, as in 2:17 and 2:25.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: the work of Christ
decisions.reason: Manuscripts differ over the name here. The sense is the same: the work of the gospel. No footnote.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: because you were far away
alternatives: what was lacking in your service
decisions.reason: Readable states why the church could not serve Paul itself, following meaning decision m4, so that the verse is not heard as a rebuke. This adds a reason the Greek leaves implicit.

decisions.choice: staking his life
decisions.reason: Keeps the gambling picture of the Greek word.
